Combination and decomposition reactions are the reverse of each other. Calcium oxide and carbon dioxide combine to form calcium carbonate, and heating calcium carbonate decomposes it back into calcium oxide and carbon dioxide — one reaction undoes the other.

More Reactions From This Unit

  • Methane burning: CH4 + 2O2 → CO2 + 2H2O
  • Magnesium burning: 2Mg + O2 → 2MgO
  • White wash chemistry: CaO + H2O → Ca(OH)2, then Ca(OH)2 + CO2 → CaCO3 + H2O on the wall
  • Cheese making: milk protein (casein) coagulates into curd when vinegar or lemon juice is added — a chemical change

Key Points

  • Combination: many substances join to form one compound (A + B → AB).
  • Decomposition: one compound splits into simpler substances (AB → A + B).
  • Combination and decomposition are reverse reactions of each other.
  • Heating KClO3 gives KCl and oxygen; heating CaCO3 gives CaO and CO2.
  • CaO + CO2 → CaCO3 is an addition (combination) reaction.

mcqs.q: The reaction between calcium oxide and carbon dioxide to form calcium carbonate is an example of:
mcqs.why: In CaO + CO2 → CaCO3, two substances combine to form a single compound. Reactions of the type A + B → AB are called addition or combination reactions.

mcqs.q: Thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate produces a gas:
mcqs.why: On heating, CaCO3 → CaO + CO2. The single compound splits into calcium oxide and carbon dioxide gas, which is a decomposition reaction.

mcqs.q: Heating of solid potassium chlorate produces a gas:
mcqs.why: Potassium chlorate decomposes on heating: 2KClO3 → 2KCl + 3O2. The gas released in this decomposition is oxygen.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a combination reaction?
mcqs.why: Carbon and oxygen are two separate substances combining into one compound, carbon dioxide. The first and third options are decompositions, and the last is a metal-acid reaction.

mcqs.q: Combination and decomposition reactions are related because they are:
mcqs.why: Combination joins substances (A + B → AB) while decomposition splits a compound (AB → A + B). For example CaO + CO2 → CaCO3 is undone by CaCO3 → CaO + CO2.

mcqs.q: The reaction Fe + S → FeS, forming iron sulphide, is a:
mcqs.why: Iron and sulphur are two separate substances that join on heating to form one compound, iron sulphide, so it is a combination reaction of the type A + B → AB.

mcqs.q: Ammonia is formed by N2 + 3H2 → 2NH3. This is an example of a:
mcqs.why: Nitrogen and hydrogen combine to form a single product, ammonia. Two reactants giving one compound is the pattern of a combination reaction.

mcqs.q: In white washing, the hard white layer on the wall forms when slaked lime reacts with:
mcqs.why: Ca(OH)2 + CO2 → CaCO3 + H2O. The slaked lime slowly takes carbon dioxide from the air and forms a hard white layer of calcium carbonate on the wall.

mcqs.q: Quicklime mixed with water gives slaked lime: CaO + H2O → Ca(OH)2. This reaction is a:
mcqs.why: Calcium oxide and water are two substances combining to form one compound, calcium hydroxide, so the reaction follows the combination pattern A + B → AB.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a decomposition reaction?
mcqs.why: One compound, potassium chlorate, splits into two simpler substances, potassium chloride and oxygen. The other options all join substances together, so they are combinations.

lessons.title: Exothermic and Endothermic Reactions
lessons.notes_html:
Exothermic Reactions

Exothermic reactions are chemical reactions during which heat is evolved (released). Examples: burning of carbon, burning of methane (CH4 + 2O2 → CO2 + 2H2O + heat), and the formation of iron sulphide from iron and sulphur (Fe + S → FeS + heat). Slaking of lime, CaO + H2O → Ca(OH)2, also evolves heat.

Endothermic Reactions

Endothermic reactions are chemical reactions during which heat is absorbed. Examples: the thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate into calcium oxide and carbon dioxide, and the formation of nitric oxide from nitrogen and oxygen (N2 + O2 → 2NO, heat absorbed).

Electricity From an Exothermic Reaction

In a thermal power station, a fuel like coal, oil or natural gas is burnt. Burning is an exothermic reaction which releases a large amount of heat. This heat boils water to produce high-pressure steam; the steam turns the turbines, and the turbines run the generators which produce electricity. In this way the chemical energy of the fuel is converted, through the heat of an exothermic reaction, into electrical energy.

Key Points

  • Exothermic reactions release heat; endothermic reactions absorb heat.
  • Burning of fuels and formation of iron sulphide are exothermic.
  • Decomposition of calcium carbonate and formation of nitric oxide are endothermic.
  • Thermal power stations use exothermic burning to make steam and electricity.
  • Slaking of quicklime with water evolves heat.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is an exothermic reaction?
options: Formation of iron sulphide by heating the mixture of iron and sulphur
Formation of nitric oxide by heating the mixture of nitrogen and oxygen
Formation of hydrogen iodide by heating the mixture of hydrogen and iodine
Formation of calcium oxide and carbon dioxide by heating calcium carbonate
mcqs.why: Once started, Fe + S → FeS continues on its own and gives out heat, so it is exothermic. Forming nitric oxide and decomposing calcium carbonate absorb heat, so they are endothermic. The book key is correct.

mcqs.q: An exothermic reaction is one in which:
mcqs.why: By definition, exothermic reactions release heat to the surroundings, like the burning of carbon or methane. Reactions that take in heat are called endothermic.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is an endothermic reaction?
mcqs.why: CaCO3 → CaO + CO2 only proceeds while heat is continuously supplied and absorbed. Burning reactions and iron sulphide formation release heat, so they are exothermic.

mcqs.q: The formation of nitric oxide, N2 + O2 → 2NO, is endothermic because it:
mcqs.why: Nitrogen and oxygen combine to form nitric oxide only when heat is taken in, for example at very high temperatures. Heat absorption is the mark of an endothermic reaction.

mcqs.q: In a thermal power station, electricity is generated with the help of an exothermic reaction because burning fuel:
options: Releases heat that boils water to make steam for turbines
mcqs.why: Burning coal, oil or gas releases heat, which makes high-pressure steam. The steam turns turbines connected to generators, converting chemical energy into electrical energy.

mcqs.q: Burning of methane, CH4 + 2O2 → CO2 + 2H2O + heat, is classified as:
mcqs.why: Heat appears on the product side of the equation: the reaction gives out heat as methane burns. Any reaction that evolves heat is exothermic.

mcqs.q: When quicklime is mixed with water to prepare white wash, the mixture becomes hot because the reaction:
mcqs.why: CaO + H2O → Ca(OH)2 releases heat as slaked lime forms, so the mixture warms up. A reaction that evolves heat is an exothermic reaction.

mcqs.q: Which pair contains only exothermic reactions?
options: Burning of carbon and formation of iron sulphide
Decomposition of CaCO3 and formation of NO
Formation of NO and burning of carbon
Decomposition of CaCO3 and burning of methane
mcqs.why: Both burning of carbon and Fe + S → FeS give out heat. Decomposition of calcium carbonate and formation of nitric oxide absorb heat, so any pair containing them is wrong.

mcqs.q: An endothermic reaction can be recognized because, during the reaction, heat is:
mcqs.why: Endothermic reactions absorb heat, so continuous heating is usually needed to keep them going, as when calcium carbonate is heated to form calcium oxide and carbon dioxide.

mcqs.q: The heat released by burning fuel in a power station is used to:
mcqs.why: The exothermic burning heats water into high-pressure steam. The steam drives the turbines, and the turbines run the generators that produce electricity.

lessons.title: Acids and Their Properties
lessons.notes_html:
What Is an Acid?

An acid is a substance which has a sour taste, turns blue litmus red, and produces hydrogen ions (protons) in water. Acids react with active metals to produce salts and hydrogen gas, and they neutralize bases to form salts and water.

Properties of Acids

  • They have a sour taste.
  • They turn blue litmus red.
  • They react with active metals to produce a salt and hydrogen gas.
  • They react with metal carbonates to liberate carbon dioxide.
  • They neutralize bases to form salt and water, and their aqueous solutions conduct electricity.

Mineral Acids

Three mineral acids are hydrochloric acid (HCl), sulphuric acid (H2SO4) — called the king of chemicals — and nitric acid (HNO3). They are called mineral acids because they are prepared from minerals in industries and laboratories.

Acids in Food

  • Citric acid — in citrus fruits, especially lemon and orange
  • Tartaric acid — in tamarind (imli) and unripe grapes
  • Acetic acid — in vinegar (about 5-8% acetic acid in water), prepared by the fermentation of sugars
  • Lactic acid — in yogurt

These food acids are weak organic acids and are safe in small quantities. Hydrochloric and sulphuric acids are strong mineral acids: highly corrosive and very dangerous for human health.

Strength and Basicity

A sulphuric acid molecule can give two protons in water while a hydrochloric acid molecule gives only one, but that does not make sulphuric acid twice as strong. The strength of an acid depends on how completely it ionizes in water, while the number of protons it can give is its basicity. H2SO4 is a dibasic acid and HCl is monobasic; both are strong acids.

Key Points

  • Acids taste sour and turn blue litmus red.
  • Sulphuric acid (H2SO4) is called the king of chemicals.
  • Acids react with active metals to give a salt and hydrogen gas.
  • Citric acid is in lemons, tartaric acid in tamarind, acetic acid in vinegar, lactic acid in yogurt.
  • Acid strength depends on ionization, not on the number of protons.

mcqs.q: The king of chemicals is:
mcqs.why: Sulphuric acid (H2SO4) is called the king of chemicals because of its very wide use in industries. HCl is another strong acid, KOH is a base and NaCl is a salt.

mcqs.q: Lactic acid is found in:
mcqs.why: Lactic acid is the acid present in yogurt (and sour milk), formed when bacteria ferment the milk sugar. Grapes contain tartaric acid and vinegar contains acetic acid.

mcqs.q: An acid can be identified because it turns:
mcqs.why: Acids turn blue litmus red — this is a standard test for an acid. Bases do the opposite and turn red litmus blue.

mcqs.q: When an acid reacts with an active metal, the gas produced is:
mcqs.why: Acids react with active metals to produce a salt and hydrogen gas, for example Mg + 2HCl → MgCl2 + H2. The gas burns with a pop sound.

mcqs.q: Citric acid is found in:
mcqs.why: Citric acid occurs in citrus fruits, especially lemon and orange. Tamarind has tartaric acid, vinegar has acetic acid and yogurt has lactic acid.

mcqs.q: Tartaric acid is found in:
mcqs.why: Tartaric acid is the acid of tamarind (imli) and unripe grapes, which is why both taste sharply sour before the grapes ripen.

mcqs.q: Acetic acid is present in:
mcqs.why: Vinegar is about 5-8% acetic acid in water, prepared by the fermentation of sugars. Its sour smell and taste come from acetic acid.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a mineral acid?
mcqs.why: Nitric acid (HNO3), along with HCl and H2SO4, is a mineral acid prepared from minerals in industries and laboratories. Citric, acetic and lactic acids are organic acids from food sources.

mcqs.q: Sulphuric acid can give two protons and HCl only one. This means sulphuric acid is:
options: Not necessarily stronger; strength depends on ionization
mcqs.why: Strength depends on how completely an acid ionizes in water, not on proton count. H2SO4 is dibasic and HCl monobasic, but both ionize almost completely and are strong acids.

mcqs.q: When an acid reacts with a metal carbonate, the gas liberated is:
mcqs.why: Acids react with metal carbonates to liberate carbon dioxide, for example 2NaHCO3 + H2SO4 → Na2SO4 + 2H2O + 2CO2, seen as brisk effervescence.

lessons.title: Bases, Alkalis and Indicators
lessons.notes_html:
Bases and Alkalis

A base produces hydroxide ions (OH-) in water and neutralizes acids. A base that dissolves in water is called an alkali. Sodium hydroxide (NaOH), commonly called caustic soda, is the alkali used in drain cleaners to open a blocked drain, because it dissolves grease, hair and other organic matter.

Ammonia and Water

Ammonia dissolves in water to form ammonium hydroxide, which is an alkali and turns red litmus blue: NH3 + H2O → NH4OH.

Indicators

An indicator is a substance that shows different colours in acids and bases. Litmus solution is prepared from lichens: the lichens are crushed, their purple dye is extracted in water and the solution is filtered. Blue and red litmus papers are made by soaking filter paper strips in it and drying them. Phenolphthalein gives a pink colour with a sodium hydroxide solution. Using pH paper: vinegar has pH about 3 (acidic), milk about 6.5 (slightly acidic), and a common salt solution has pH 7 (neutral).

Why Water Is Neutral

An acid produces hydrogen ions (H+) in water and a base produces hydroxide ions (OH-). Water produces equal numbers of H+ and OH- ions (H2O → H+ + OH-), so it is neither acidic nor basic. It does not change the colour of litmus and its pH is 7, so water is called a neutral compound.

Basic Salt Solutions

The aqueous solutions of NaHCO3 and Na2CO3 are basic in nature because these salts come from a strong base (NaOH) and a weak acid (carbonic acid); in water they hydrolyse and produce hydroxide ions, turning red litmus blue.

Key Points

  • Soluble bases are called alkalis; NaOH is caustic soda, used in drain cleaners.
  • Ammonia + water forms ammonium hydroxide: NH3 + H2O → NH4OH.
  • Litmus is prepared from lichens; phenolphthalein turns pink in NaOH solution.
  • Water is neutral (pH 7) because it gives equal H+ and OH- ions.
  • Salts of strong bases and weak acids give basic solutions.

mcqs.q: Sodium hydroxide solution in water will:
options: Give red colour with methyl orange
mcqs.why: Phenolphthalein is colourless in acids but turns pink in bases and alkalis like NaOH. As a base, NaOH turns red litmus blue, not blue litmus red.

mcqs.q: The alkali commonly used to open a blocked drain is:
mcqs.why: Sodium hydroxide (NaOH), caustic soda, is used in drain cleaners because it dissolves the grease, hair and other organic matter that block the drain.

mcqs.q: Ammonia reacts with water to form:
mcqs.why: NH3 + H2O → NH4OH. The ammonium hydroxide formed is an alkali, which is why ammonia solution turns red litmus blue.

mcqs.q: Litmus solution is prepared from:
mcqs.why: Litmus is a purple dye obtained from lichens. The lichens are crushed, the dye is extracted in water and filtered; litmus papers are made by soaking strips in this solution.

mcqs.q: Water is called a neutral compound because it produces:
options: Equal numbers of H+ and OH- ions
mcqs.why: Water ionizes as H2O → H+ + OH- in equal amounts, so it is neither acidic nor basic. It does not change litmus colour and has pH 7.

mcqs.q: The pH of a common salt solution is:
mcqs.why: Common salt (NaCl) is a salt of a strong acid (HCl) and a strong base (NaOH), so its solution is neutral with pH 7. Vinegar is about 3 and milk about 6.5.

mcqs.q: Ammonium hydroxide solution turns:
mcqs.why: Ammonium hydroxide is an alkali (a base), and bases turn red litmus blue. Turning blue litmus red is the test for an acid, not a base.

mcqs.q: The aqueous solution of sodium carbonate is basic because the salt is formed from:
options: A strong acid and a weak base
A weak acid and a strong base
A strong acid and a strong base
A weak acid and a weak base
mcqs.why: Na2CO3 comes from carbonic acid (weak) and sodium hydroxide (strong base). In water it hydrolyses to produce OH- ions, so the solution is basic and turns red litmus blue.

mcqs.q: Vinegar shows a pH of about 3 on pH paper because it contains:
mcqs.why: Vinegar is a dilute solution of acetic acid, so it is acidic with pH about 3, well below the neutral value of 7.

mcqs.q: A soluble base is called:
mcqs.why: Bases that dissolve in water are called alkalis, for example sodium hydroxide and ammonium hydroxide. They produce hydroxide ions in solution and turn red litmus blue.

lessons.title: Salts and Neutralization
lessons.notes_html:
Neutralization

When an acid reacts with a base, they neutralize each other and form a salt and water. Copper oxide (a base) reacts with dilute sulphuric acid to form blue-coloured copper sulphate and water: CuO + H2SO4 → CuSO4 + H2O.

Preparing Salts — Reactions From This Unit

  • Mg + 2HCl → MgCl2 + H2 (magnesium with dilute HCl)
  • 2NaHCO3 + H2SO4 → Na2SO4 + 2H2O + 2CO2 (brisk effervescence)
  • 2Na + Cl2 → 2NaCl (sodium burns in chlorine to form common salt)
  • Sodium carbonate is obtained when carbonic acid reacts with sodium hydroxide

The Lime Water Test

When carbon dioxide gas is passed through lime water, it turns milky. The milkiness is due to the formation of insoluble calcium carbonate (CaCO3).

Salts in Water: Acidic and Basic Solutions

Copper sulphate is a salt of a weak base (copper hydroxide) and a strong acid (sulphuric acid), so its solution is acidic and turns blue litmus slightly red. In general, salts of strong acids and weak bases give acidic solutions, while salts of weak acids and strong bases give basic solutions.

Which Acid and Base Make a Salt?

  • Calcium acetate — acetic acid + calcium hydroxide
  • Potassium hydrogen sulphate — sulphuric acid + potassium hydroxide (an acid salt, only one hydrogen replaced)
  • Magnesium nitrate — nitric acid + magnesium hydroxide
  • Ammonium oxalate — oxalic acid + ammonium hydroxide
  • Sodium potassium tartrate (Rochelle salt) — tartaric acid + sodium hydroxide and potassium hydroxide
  • Ferric chloride — hydrochloric acid + iron(III) hydroxide

Key Points

  • Acid + base → salt + water; this is neutralization.
  • CO2 turns lime water milky due to insoluble CaCO3.
  • Copper sulphate solution is acidic (weak base + strong acid salt).
  • CuO + H2SO4 → CuSO4 + H2O gives blue copper sulphate.
  • Every salt can be traced back to a parent acid and a parent base.

mcqs.q: When carbon dioxide gas is passed through lime water, the milkiness is due to the compound:
mcqs.why: Carbon dioxide reacts with lime water to form insoluble calcium carbonate, CaCO3, whose fine white particles make the lime water look milky. This is the standard test for CO2.

mcqs.q: Sodium carbonate is an important industrial salt. Which acid is reacted with sodium hydroxide to get it?
mcqs.why: Sodium carbonate contains the carbonate part of carbonic acid (H2CO3). Neutralizing carbonic acid with sodium hydroxide gives sodium carbonate and water.

mcqs.q: Copper oxide reacts with dilute sulphuric acid to form:
mcqs.why: CuO + H2SO4 → CuSO4 + H2O. Copper oxide is a base, so this is a neutralization; the blue colour of the solution confirms copper sulphate formation.

mcqs.q: Magnesium reacts with dilute HCl to form:
mcqs.why: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl2 + H2. Magnesium is an active metal, so it reacts vigorously with the acid to give the salt magnesium chloride and hydrogen gas.

mcqs.q: When sodium hydrogen carbonate reacts with dilute H2SO4, the brisk effervescence is due to:
mcqs.why: 2NaHCO3 + H2SO4 → Na2SO4 + 2H2O + 2CO2. The bubbles of carbon dioxide released cause the brisk effervescence seen in this reaction.

mcqs.q: Sodium burns in chlorine to form:
mcqs.why: 2Na + Cl2 → 2NaCl. The metal sodium combines directly with chlorine gas to form sodium chloride, which is common salt.

mcqs.q: A solution of copper sulphate turns blue litmus slightly red because copper sulphate is a salt of:
options: A strong base and a weak acid
A strong acid and a strong base
A weak base and a strong acid
A weak acid and a weak base
mcqs.why: Copper sulphate comes from copper hydroxide (weak base) and sulphuric acid (strong acid). Such salts hydrolyse in water to give acidic solutions.

mcqs.q: Ferric chloride is prepared from hydrochloric acid and:
mcqs.why: The base used with hydrochloric acid to make ferric chloride is ferric hydroxide, that is iron(III) hydroxide. Acid + base neutralization gives the salt plus water.

mcqs.q: Potassium hydrogen sulphate is called an acid salt because:
options: Only one hydrogen of sulphuric acid is replaced
mcqs.why: Sulphuric acid has two replaceable hydrogens. In potassium hydrogen sulphate only one is replaced by potassium, so the salt still holds an acidic hydrogen — an acid salt.

mcqs.q: The reaction acid + base → salt + water is called:
mcqs.why: In neutralization the acid and base cancel each other's effect, forming a salt and water, for example CuO + H2SO4 → CuSO4 + H2O.

lessons.title: Acids, Bases and Salts in Daily Life
lessons.notes_html:
Salts in Industry

  • Sodium carbonate (washing soda): used in the glass, soap and paper industries and as a water softener
  • Sodium chloride (common salt): used in the manufacture of sodium hydroxide, chlorine and soda ash, and in food preservation
  • Calcium carbonate: used in the cement industry
  • Copper sulphate: used as a fungicide

Salts and the Human Body

Common salt (NaCl) maintains the balance of water and electrolytes in the body and is needed for the working of nerves and muscles. Calcium salts build strong bones and teeth, iron salts are needed to make haemoglobin of blood, and iodine salt keeps the thyroid gland healthy and prevents goitre. Salts in ORS replace the salts lost in diarrhoea and save life.

Treating Stomach Acidity

Sodium hydrogen carbonate (baking soda, NaHCO3) is used in antacids to reduce acidity in the stomach. It neutralizes the excess hydrochloric acid: NaHCO3 + HCl → NaCl + H2O + CO2. Potassium bicarbonate (KHCO3) can also be used for baking cakes, because on heating it releases carbon dioxide (2KHCO3 → K2CO3 + H2O + CO2), which makes the cake rise and become soft and spongy.

Copper Sulphate and Pink Salt

Copper sulphate (CuSO4), called blue vitriol or neela thotha, kills fungus and algae in plants and trees; sprayed with lime as Bordeaux mixture, it protects crops from fungal diseases. The common salt of the Khewra mines is pink because of impurities, mainly traces of iron compounds mixed with the sodium chloride; pure sodium chloride is white.

Soil Problems

Soil becomes acidic from excessive chemical fertilizers, acid rain, decomposing organic matter and continuous cropping that removes basic minerals. Acidic garden soil is treated by adding a base — slaked lime, quicklime or powdered chalk — which neutralizes the excess acid. White salt crusts on soil (salinity) are removed by leaching with water and good drainage, adding gypsum and organic manure, and growing salt-tolerant plants.

Key Points

  • NaHCO3 in antacids neutralizes excess stomach acid.
  • Iron salts make haemoglobin; calcium salts build bones and teeth; iodine prevents goitre.
  • Copper sulphate (blue vitriol) is a fungicide for plants.
  • Khewra salt is pink due to iron compound impurities.
  • Acidic soil is treated with lime; saline soil by leaching, drainage and gypsum.

mcqs.q: Which salt is used in antacids to reduce acidity in the stomach?
mcqs.why: NaHCO3 (baking soda) neutralizes the excess hydrochloric acid in the stomach: NaHCO3 + HCl → NaCl + H2O + CO2, giving relief from acidity.

mcqs.q: Copper sulphate, used to kill fungus and algae in plants, is commonly called:
mcqs.why: Copper sulphate (CuSO4) is known as blue vitriol or neela thotha. Sprayed on crops, often with lime as Bordeaux mixture, it protects plants from fungal diseases.

mcqs.q: The common salt of the Khewra mines is pink in colour because of:
options: Traces of iron compounds as impurities
mcqs.why: Pure sodium chloride is white. The pink shade of Khewra rock salt (Himalayan pink salt) comes from mineral impurities, mainly traces of iron oxide mixed in the rock.

mcqs.q: Iron salts are needed by the human body to make:
mcqs.why: Iron is an essential part of haemoglobin, the red pigment that carries oxygen in blood. Calcium salts build bones and teeth, while iodine keeps the thyroid healthy.

mcqs.q: Iodized salt prevents the disease:
mcqs.why: Iodine (added as potassium iodide) is needed by the thyroid gland. A lack of iodine causes the thyroid to swell, a condition called goitre, so iodized salt prevents it.

mcqs.q: Potassium bicarbonate can be used for baking cakes because, like baking soda, on heating it releases:
mcqs.why: 2KHCO3 → K2CO3 + H2O + CO2. The carbon dioxide bubbles make the cake rise and become soft and spongy, exactly the job baking soda does.

mcqs.q: Acidic garden soil is made fit for growing vegetables by adding:
mcqs.why: Slaked lime (calcium hydroxide) is a base. It neutralizes the excess acid in the soil and brings the pH close to 7, after which vegetables grow well.

mcqs.q: Sodium carbonate (washing soda) is used in industries for making:
mcqs.why: Sodium carbonate is an important industrial salt used in the glass, soap and paper industries, and also as a water softener in washing.

mcqs.q: Soil becomes acidic mainly due to:
options: Excessive chemical fertilizers and acid rain
mcqs.why: Heavy use of fertilizers like ammonium sulphate, acid rain, decomposing organic matter and continuous cropping that removes basic minerals all make soil acidic over time.

mcqs.q: The white salt crust on kitchen-garden soil (salinity) can be removed by:
options: Leaching with water, good drainage and adding gypsum
mcqs.why: Heavy watering dissolves the excess salts and washes them below the roots, drainage carries the salty water away, and gypsum helps remove sodium salts from saline soil.

lessons.title: Balanced and Unbalanced Forces
lessons.notes_html:
Balanced Forces

Balanced forces are equal in size and opposite in direction, so their net (resultant) force is zero. They cannot change the state of motion of an object: a stationary object remains stationary, and a moving object keeps moving with the same speed in the same direction. Two equal forces acting at the same time on a stationary object in opposite directions leave the object stationary.

Unbalanced Forces

Only an unbalanced force can produce a change in motion — starting, stopping, speeding up, slowing down or changing direction. If two forces act in opposite directions, the net force equals the difference of the two forces and acts in the direction of the larger force: 10 N to the right and 6 N to the left give a net force of 4 N to the right.

The Normal Force

The normal force is the upward force exerted by a surface on an object resting on it. It is balanced by the weight (force of gravity) of the object acting downward. A book lying on a table stays at rest because the table pushes it up with a normal force equal to its weight. When a student pushes a tree with 10 N and the tree does not move, the tree also exerts 10 N back on the student — the forces are balanced.

A Slowing Car and a Paratrooper

A car slowing down does not experience balanced forces: the backward forces (brake friction, air resistance, rolling friction) are greater than the forward engine force, so the net force is backward. A paratrooper falls under two forces — weight downward and air resistance upward. At first the forces are unbalanced and he speeds up; when air resistance grows equal to his weight, the forces become balanced and he falls at a steady speed. Balanced forces do not stop him: he was already moving downward, so he keeps falling at that constant speed until he lands.

Key Points

  • Balanced forces: equal, opposite, net force zero — no change in motion.
  • Only unbalanced forces can change an object's motion.
  • Net force of opposite forces = difference, in the direction of the larger force.
  • The normal force of a surface balances the weight of a resting object.
  • A slowing car and a speeding-up paratrooper both have unbalanced forces.

mcqs.q: Two equal forces act at the same time on the same stationary object but in opposite directions. The object:
mcqs.why: Equal and opposite forces are balanced, so the net force is zero. Balanced forces cannot change the motion of an object, so a stationary object remains stationary.

mcqs.q: A student pushes against a tree with a force of 10 newtons (N). The tree does not move. The force exerted by the tree on the student is:
mcqs.why: The tree pushes back with an equal force of 10 N in the opposite direction, so the forces are balanced and nothing moves. The book key is correct.

mcqs.q: What causes objects to change their motion?
mcqs.why: A change in motion — starting, stopping, speeding up, slowing down or turning — happens only when the net force is not zero, that is, when forces are unbalanced.

mcqs.q: Can a balanced force produce a change in motion?
options: Yes, if the object is heavy
mcqs.why: Balanced forces have a net force of zero, exactly as if no force acted. A stationary object stays at rest and a moving object keeps its speed and direction unchanged.

mcqs.q: A force of 10 N acts to the right and 6 N to the left on an object. The net force is:
mcqs.why: For opposite forces the net force is the difference: 10 − 6 = 4 N. It acts in the direction of the larger force, which is to the right.

mcqs.q: A book resting on a table stays at rest because the normal force of the table:
mcqs.why: The table pushes the book up with a normal force equal to the book's weight pulling it down. The two forces balance, the net force is zero, and the book stays at rest.

mcqs.q: A car that is slowing down experiences:
mcqs.why: Slowing down is a change in motion, which needs a net force. The backward forces of brakes, air resistance and rolling friction exceed the forward engine force, so the forces are unbalanced.

mcqs.q: When the air resistance on a falling paratrooper becomes equal to his weight, he:
options: Falls at a steady constant speed
mcqs.why: Equal upward air resistance and downward weight are balanced forces, so his motion stops changing. He continues falling at the same constant (terminal) speed and lands safely.

mcqs.q: If balanced forces act on a moving object, the object will:
options: Keep moving with the same speed and direction
mcqs.why: Balanced forces prevent any change in motion; they do not cancel motion itself. The paratrooper keeps falling at constant speed for this very reason.

mcqs.q: Just after a parachute opens, the paratrooper accelerates downward because:
options: Air resistance is greater than his weight
His weight is greater than the air resistance
mcqs.why: At first the upward air resistance is smaller than the downward weight, so the forces are unbalanced with a net downward force, and he accelerates downward until the forces balance.

lessons.title: Pressure: Force per Unit Area
lessons.notes_html:
What Is Pressure?

Pressure is the force acting per unit area of a surface: Pressure = Force / Area, or P = F/A. Its SI unit is the pascal (Pa), which is equal to one newton per square metre (N/m2). The same force exerts more pressure on a smaller area and less pressure on a larger area.

Worked Example

A force of 1800 N acts on a surface area of 0.06 m2. P = F/A = 1800 / 0.06 = 30,000 Pa = 30 kPa. In the same way, a force of 600 N on 0.02 m2 gives P = 600 / 0.02 = 30,000 Pa, while 100 N spread over 2 m2 gives only P = 100 / 2 = 50 Pa.

The Camel in the Desert

A bulky camel travels easily in deserts because it has large, broad and padded feet. Its heavy weight (force) is spread over the large area of its feet, so the pressure on the sand is small (P = F/A) and its feet do not sink into the soft sand. That is why the camel is called the ship of the desert.

Pressure in Fluids — Pascal's Principle (Project)

The hydraulic brake model shows Pascal's principle: pressure applied at one point on an incompressible fluid in a closed container is transmitted equally to all points of the fluid. Pushing the master syringe piston applies pressure on the fluid, which transmits it equally to the other syringes so their pistons move out together — just as pressing a brake pedal sends pressure through brake fluid to the cylinders of all four wheels.

Key Points

  • Pressure = Force / Area (P = F/A); SI unit is the pascal (Pa = N/m2).
  • Smaller area, same force → higher pressure; larger area → lower pressure.
  • 1800 N on 0.06 m2 gives 30,000 Pa = 30 kPa.
  • Broad feet spread the camel's weight, so pressure on sand stays small.
  • Pascal's principle: fluid pressure is transmitted equally in all directions.

mcqs.q: The SI unit of pressure is:
mcqs.why: Pressure is measured in pascals (Pa), where 1 Pa = 1 N/m2. Watt is the unit of power, joule of energy and newton of force.

mcqs.q: When the same amount of force is applied on different areas, it exerts:
mcqs.why: Pressure = Force / Area. With the force fixed, dividing by a smaller area gives a larger pressure, which is why a sharp point presses in more easily than a blunt one.

mcqs.q: A force of 1800 N is acting on a surface area of 0.06 m2. The pressure exerted will be:
mcqs.why: P = F/A = 1800 / 0.06 = 30,000 Pa. Converting to kilopascals, 30,000 Pa = 30 kPa. The book key is correct.

mcqs.q: Pressure is defined as:
mcqs.why: Pressure = Force / Area (P = F/A). It tells how concentrated a force is on a surface and is measured in pascals (N/m2).

mcqs.q: A force of 600 N acts on an area of 0.02 m2. The pressure is:
mcqs.why: P = F/A = 600 / 0.02 = 30,000 Pa = 30 kPa. A small area concentrates the force, giving a high pressure even with a moderate force.

mcqs.q: A bulky camel walks easily on desert sand because its broad feet:
options: Reduce the pressure on the sand by spreading the force over a large area
Increase the pressure on the sand
mcqs.why: Pressure = Force / Area. The camel's large padded feet spread its heavy weight over a big area, so the pressure is small and the feet do not sink into soft sand.

mcqs.q: If the area on which a force acts is doubled (force unchanged), the pressure becomes:
mcqs.why: P = F/A, so pressure is inversely proportional to area. Doubling the area with the same force halves the pressure: for example 100 N on 2 m2 gives only 50 Pa.

mcqs.q: One pascal is equal to:
mcqs.why: By definition 1 Pa = 1 N/m2, because pressure is force divided by area. This is the SI unit named after Blaise Pascal.

mcqs.q: The hydraulic brake model works on Pascal's principle, which states that pressure applied to a fluid in a closed container is:
options: Transmitted equally to all points of the fluid
mcqs.why: Pushing the master syringe transmits the same pressure through the fluid to every other syringe, moving all pistons together — the same principle used in vehicle brakes.

mcqs.q: A force of 100 N is spread over an area of 2 m2. The pressure exerted is:
mcqs.why: P = F/A = 100 / 2 = 50 Pa. Spreading a force over a large area gives a small pressure, the opposite of concentrating it on a small area.

lessons.title: Liquid and Atmospheric Pressure
lessons.notes_html:
Pressure in Liquids

The pressure at the bottom of a tank containing a liquid depends on the height of the liquid column, the nature of the liquid (its density) and the acceleration due to gravity. It does not depend on the area of the bottom surface. A taller column of liquid presses down with more weight, so pressure grows with depth.

Floating and Sinking

Whether an object floats or sinks does not depend directly on its size; it depends on density and the upthrust of the liquid. An object floats if its average density is less than the density of the liquid, and sinks if its density is greater. That is why a huge steel ship, whose average density including the air inside is less than water, floats, while a small iron nail sinks.

Atmospheric Pressure

The air around us presses on everything with atmospheric pressure. As we go up in the air, atmospheric pressure decreases, because the column of air above becomes shorter and the air becomes thinner. People on hills therefore experience atmospheric pressure less than that at sea level.

Where Is Pressure Lowest?

In a landscape with the sea, shore points, a low hollow and a high mountain peak, the atmospheric pressure is lowest at the top of the mountain peak. Pressure is highest near sea level, higher in the low hollow than on the peak, and lowest at the highest point.

Key Points

  • Liquid pressure depends on height of the column, nature of the liquid and gravity — not on the area of the bottom.
  • Floating or sinking depends on density, not on size alone.
  • Atmospheric pressure decreases as we go up; hills have lower pressure than sea level.
  • Atmospheric pressure is lowest at the highest point, such as a mountain peak.
  • Air gets thinner with height, so the air column above becomes shorter.

mcqs.q: The pressure at the bottom of a tank containing a liquid does not depend on:
mcqs.why: Liquid pressure depends on the height of the liquid column, the density (nature) of the liquid and gravity. The area of the bottom does not affect the pressure at a given depth.

mcqs.q: People on hills experience atmospheric pressure:
options: More than that at sea level
Less than that at sea level
Same as that at sea level
Four times more than at sea level
mcqs.why: Atmospheric pressure decreases with height because the column of air above is shorter and thinner. Hills are higher than sea level, so the pressure there is less.

mcqs.q: As we go up in the air:
options: Atmospheric pressure becomes zero at 1 km
mcqs.why: Going up means less air above pressing down and thinner air, so atmospheric pressure falls steadily with height, though it does not reach zero at 1 km.

mcqs.q: In a scene with the sea, shore points, a low hollow and a high mountain peak, atmospheric pressure is lowest at:
options: The top of the mountain peak
mcqs.why: The peak is the highest point, where the air column above is shortest and the air thinnest, so atmospheric pressure there is the lowest of all the locations.

mcqs.q: The pressure at the bottom of a liquid tank increases when:
options: The height of the liquid column increases
The area of the bottom increases
mcqs.why: A taller liquid column has more weight pressing down, so the pressure at the bottom increases. The bottom area does not change the pressure at that depth.

mcqs.q: A huge steel ship floats on water while a small iron nail sinks, because floating depends on:
options: The average density of the object compared with the liquid
mcqs.why: The ship's average density, including the air inside its hull, is less than water, so it floats. The solid nail is denser than water, so it sinks despite being small.

mcqs.q: Atmospheric pressure decreases with height because:
options: The air column above becomes shorter and the air thinner
mcqs.why: Pressure comes from the weight of air above. Higher up there is less air overhead and it is less dense, so the pressure it exerts is smaller.

mcqs.q: Which of these does the pressure at the bottom of a liquid tank depend on?
mcqs.why: A denser liquid weighs more for the same column height, so it exerts more pressure. Liquid pressure depends on column height, the nature of the liquid and gravity.

mcqs.q: At which place is atmospheric pressure expected to be the highest?
options: In an aeroplane at high altitude
mcqs.why: Sea level is the lowest of these places, with the full column of air above it, so atmospheric pressure is greatest there and decreases as we climb.

mcqs.q: An object will float in a liquid if its average density is:
mcqs.why: Floating requires the upthrust to balance the weight, which happens when the object's average density is less than the liquid's density. Denser objects sink.

chapters.title: Unit 9 — Reflection and Refraction of Light

lessons.title: How Light Behaves: Transmission, Absorption and Reflection
lessons.notes_html:
Light Passing Through Materials

When light falls on a material, different things can happen to it. Transmission is the passing of light through a material. Light passes through transparent objects such as clear glass, and this passing is called transmission.

Absorption is different. When light falls on an opaque object, especially a dark or rough one, the light is taken in and converted into heat energy. A black surface absorbs most of the light falling on it.

Reflection of Light

Reflection is the bouncing back of light from a smooth shiny surface into the same medium. When light hits a shiny or smooth surface, it is reflected. The image formed in a mirror is an example of reflection.

Why Objects Look Black or White

The colour of an object depends on the light it reflects. An object that absorbs all the light that hits it looks black. White paper reflects most of the light falling on it, while black words on a page absorb almost all the light and reflect very little. This contrast makes the black words visible to us.

Dark surfaces are good absorbers and poor reflectors of light. In sunlight, water in a black bowl becomes warmer than water in a white bowl, because the black bowl absorbs more sunlight and converts it into heat, while the white bowl reflects most of the light.

Speed of Light

Light travels at different speeds in different materials. It travels the fastest in vacuum, slower in air, and slower still in water and glass. This change of speed is important in refraction, which is studied later in this unit.

Key Points

  • Transmission is the passing of light through a transparent material.
  • Absorption takes light in and converts it into heat energy.
  • Reflection is the bouncing back of light from a smooth shiny surface.
  • An object that absorbs all light looks black, and light is fastest in vacuum.

mcqs.q: Through which of the following does light travel the fastest?
mcqs.why: Light travels fastest in vacuum because there is no material to slow it down, while air, water and glass slow it slightly.

mcqs.q: What is the colour of an object that absorbs all the light that hits it?
mcqs.why: An object that absorbs all colours of light reflects almost nothing to our eyes, so it appears black.

mcqs.q: What happens when light hits a shiny or smooth surface?
mcqs.why: A shiny or smooth surface bounces light back in an orderly way, and this bouncing back is called reflection.

mcqs.q: What is transmission of light?
options: Light bouncing back from a mirror
Light being taken in as heat
mcqs.why: Transmission means light passes through a transparent material, such as light passing through clear glass.

mcqs.q: What is absorption of light?
options: Light taken in and converted into heat energy
mcqs.why: In absorption, an opaque object takes in the light falling on it and the light energy changes into heat energy.

mcqs.q: Why do black words on white paper look visible to us?
options: The words reflect more light than the paper
The paper absorbs all light and the words reflect it
The paper reflects most light while the words absorb almost all light
The words produce their own light
mcqs.why: White paper reflects most light into our eyes while black letters reflect very little, and this contrast makes the words stand out.

mcqs.q: Two bowls with equal water are kept in sunlight. In which bowl will the water become warmer?
mcqs.why: The black bowl absorbs more sunlight and converts it into heat, while the white bowl reflects most of the light away.

mcqs.q: Which surface is a poor reflector of light?
mcqs.why: Dark rough surfaces absorb most of the light falling on them, so they reflect very little light and are poor reflectors.

mcqs.q: Light passing through clear glass is an example of which process?
mcqs.why: Clear glass is transparent, so light passes through it, and the passing of light through a material is transmission.

mcqs.q: What does a white surface do to most of the light falling on it?
options: It absorbs most of the light
It converts all light into heat
It reflects most of the light
mcqs.why: White and shiny surfaces are good reflectors that send most of the falling light back, so they absorb little and heat up slowly.

lessons.title: Reflection and Plane Mirrors
lessons.notes_html:
Laws of Reflection

Reflection follows two laws. First, the angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection. Second, the incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal, which is the perpendicular at the point of incidence, all lie in the same plane.

Image in a Plane Mirror

A plane mirror forms an image that is virtual, erect and of the same shape, size and colour as the object. The image is at the same distance behind the mirror as the object is in front of it. The image is also laterally inverted, which means it is horizontally reversed from left to right.

When we see our image, rays from our body strike the mirror and are reflected into our eyes. Every ray obeys the law of reflection. The reflected rays appear to come from a point behind the mirror, so the brain sees a virtual image there.

Seeing Each Other in a Mirror

Light paths are reversible. If person A can see person B in a mirror, then B can also see A in the same mirror, because light from each person is reflected by the mirror into the eyes of the other person with equal angles of incidence and reflection.

Uses of Lateral Inversion and Multiple Reflection

The word AMBULANCE is written as its mirror image on the front of the vehicle. A driver ahead sees it in a rear-view mirror, the mirror reverses it again, and the driver reads it correctly and gives way quickly.

A kaleidoscope uses three plane mirror strips joined into a triangular tube. Light is reflected repeatedly by the mirrors, so coloured beads form beautiful symmetrical patterns. This works on the principle of multiple reflection.

Key Points

  • The angle of incidence is always equal to the angle of reflection.
  • A plane mirror image is virtual, erect, same size and laterally inverted.
  • The image distance behind the mirror equals the object distance in front.
  • AMBULANCE is written reversed so drivers read it correctly in mirrors.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is true for an image in a plane mirror?
options: It is formed when light is blocked by an opaque object
It is formed when light passes through a transparent object
It is of the same shape, size and colour as the object
mcqs.why: A plane mirror forms a virtual, erect image that has the same shape, size and colour as the object placed in front of it.

mcqs.q: How is the angle of incidence related to the angle of reflection?
mcqs.why: The first law of reflection states that the angle of incidence is always equal to the angle of reflection.

mcqs.q: Which of the following describes the image of a boy formed by a plane mirror?
options: It will be in front of the mirror
It will be larger than the boy
It will be horizontally reversed left to right
mcqs.why: A plane mirror image is laterally inverted, so left and right are reversed while the image stays erect and the same size.

mcqs.q: According to the laws of reflection, which three lines lie in the same plane?
options: Incident ray, reflected ray and normal
mcqs.why: The second law of reflection says the incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal at the point of incidence all lie in one plane.

mcqs.q: Where is the image of an object placed 2 metres in front of a plane mirror formed?
options: On the surface of the mirror
mcqs.why: In a plane mirror the image is as far behind the mirror as the object is in front of it, so both distances are 2 metres.

mcqs.q: Why is AMBULANCE written as a mirror image on the front of the vehicle?
options: So it looks attractive from the front
So a driver ahead reads it correctly in the rear-view mirror
So it can be read from far away at night
So it is reversed for the ambulance driver
mcqs.why: The rear-view mirror reverses the writing once more, so the driver ahead reads AMBULANCE correctly and gives way quickly.

mcqs.q: If A can see B in a plane mirror, what else is true?
options: B cannot see A in the mirror
B can also see A in the mirror
The mirror blocks light from A
mcqs.why: Light paths are reversible and both follow the law of reflection, so light from A also reaches B and B can see A.

mcqs.q: A kaleidoscope forms beautiful patterns by using which principle?
mcqs.why: Three plane mirrors reflect the coloured beads again and again, producing many symmetrical images that form the patterns.

mcqs.q: The image formed by a plane mirror is described as virtual because it is formed:
options: On a screen placed behind the mirror
Where reflected rays appear to come from behind the mirror
In front of the mirror surface
mcqs.why: Reflected rays do not actually meet behind the mirror; they only appear to come from there, so the image is virtual.

mcqs.q: What is the normal in reflection?
options: The perpendicular at the point of incidence
The ray coming from the object
The ray going into the eye
mcqs.why: The normal is the line drawn perpendicular to the mirror at the point where the incident ray strikes the surface.

lessons.title: Spherical Mirrors
lessons.notes_html:
Two Types of Spherical Mirrors

Spherical mirrors have curved reflecting surfaces. A concave mirror curves inward, while a convex mirror curves outward. Their images and uses are quite different.

Images Formed by Spherical Mirrors

A concave mirror can form an image larger than the object. It mostly forms real and inverted images, which may be larger or smaller depending on the distance of the object. When the object is very close, it forms a virtual, erect and magnified image.

A convex mirror always forms a virtual, erect and diminished image behind the mirror. Because the image is smaller, the mirror gives a wider field of view.

Uses of Concave Mirrors

  • Used by dentists and doctors to see enlarged images of teeth and ears.
  • Used in torches, searchlights and car headlights to produce a strong parallel beam of light.
  • Used as shaving and makeup mirrors for a magnified image.
  • Used in solar cookers and furnaces to concentrate sunlight.

Uses of Convex Mirrors

  • Used as rear-view driving mirrors in vehicles for an erect image and wider field of view.
  • Used as security mirrors in shops and at sharp road turns.

Key Points

  • A concave mirror can form a magnified image larger than the object.
  • A convex mirror always forms a virtual, erect and diminished image.
  • Concave mirrors are used in headlights, by dentists and in solar cookers.
  • Convex mirrors are used as rear-view and security mirrors.

mcqs.q: Which type of mirror can form an image larger than the object?
mcqs.why: A concave mirror can magnify the object, especially when the object is close, while convex and plane mirrors never give a larger image.

mcqs.q: What kind of image does a convex mirror always form?
mcqs.why: A convex mirror always forms a virtual, erect and smaller image behind the mirror, whatever the position of the object.

mcqs.q: Why are convex mirrors used as rear-view mirrors in vehicles?
options: They give an erect image and a wider field of view
They form images on a screen
mcqs.why: Convex mirrors show an erect image and cover a wide area behind the vehicle, which helps the driver see more traffic.

mcqs.q: A dentist uses a concave mirror mainly to see:
options: A smaller image of the teeth
An enlarged image of the teeth
A wider view of the room
A diminished image of the teeth
mcqs.why: When held close, a concave mirror forms a virtual, erect and magnified image, so teeth and ears can be examined clearly.

mcqs.q: Concave mirrors are used in car headlights and torches to:
options: Absorb the light of the bulb
Produce a strong parallel beam of light
mcqs.why: A bulb placed at the focus of a concave mirror sends out a strong parallel beam, which lights the road far ahead.

mcqs.q: When an object is placed very close to a concave mirror, the image formed is:
mcqs.why: A very close object in front of a concave mirror gives a virtual, erect and enlarged image, as in shaving and makeup mirrors.

mcqs.q: Concave mirrors are used in solar cookers and furnaces to:
options: Reflect light away from the food
Give a wider field of view
mcqs.why: A concave mirror converges the parallel rays of sunlight to its focus, concentrating heat energy at that point.

mcqs.q: Security mirrors in shops and at sharp road turns are usually:
mcqs.why: Convex mirrors give a wide field of view, so a large area of a shop or a blind road turn can be watched in one mirror.

mcqs.q: How do most images formed by a concave mirror appear?
mcqs.why: For most object positions a concave mirror forms real and inverted images, larger or smaller according to the object distance.

mcqs.q: A shaving mirror that gives a magnified image of the face is a:
mcqs.why: A concave mirror with the face close to it forms an erect magnified image, which is why it is used for shaving and makeup.

lessons.title: Refraction, Dispersion and the Rainbow
lessons.notes_html:
Refraction of Light

Refraction is the bending of light when it passes from one transparent medium into another of different density, for example from air into water. Refraction takes place because the speed of light changes when it enters a new medium. Reflection takes place at the surface of a mirror, while refraction takes place when light enters a new medium.

Refraction in Daily Life

  • A stick or spoon placed in water looks bent at the surface.
  • A swimming pool or pond appears shallower than it really is.
  • A coin placed under water in a bowl appears raised.
  • Stars appear to twinkle due to refraction in the air.
  • Objects seen through a glass of water appear displaced or magnified.

Dispersion and the Spectrum

Dispersion is the splitting of white light into its seven colours: violet, indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange and red. It happens when white light passes through a prism. The cause is that different colours travel at different speeds in glass and are bent by different amounts. Violet bends the most and red bends the least, so the colours separate and form a spectrum.

If a second prism is placed upside down close to the first, it bends the colours in the opposite way and recombines them into white light again. This was the experiment by Newton proving that white light is made of seven colours.

Dispersion takes place in a prism but not through a glass slab. In a prism the two refracting surfaces are inclined to each other, so colours come out separated. In a glass slab the surfaces are parallel, so colours are bent back equally at the second surface and emerge together as white light.

Formation of a Rainbow

A rainbow is formed by the dispersion of sunlight in raindrops. The drops act like tiny prisms, and sunlight is refracted, internally reflected and dispersed inside them into seven colours. Two conditions are necessary: water droplets must be present in the air, and the Sun must shine from behind the observer, low in the sky, usually after rain in the morning or evening.

A rainbow is not seen at noon because the Sun is high overhead. The Sun must be low, below about 42 degrees from the horizon, for the dispersed light to reach the eyes of the observer.

Key Points

  • Refraction is the bending of light caused by a change in its speed.
  • Dispersion splits white light into seven colours in a prism.
  • Violet light bends the most and red light bends the least.
  • A rainbow needs raindrops in the air and a low Sun behind the observer.

mcqs.q: Refraction of light takes place because:
options: The speed of light changes in a new medium
Light is reflected by a mirror
mcqs.why: When light enters a medium of different density its speed changes, and this change of speed makes the light bend.

mcqs.q: A spoon placed in water looks bent at the surface. This is an example of:
mcqs.why: Light from the spoon bends as it passes from water into air, so the spoon appears bent and displaced at the surface.

mcqs.q: Why does a swimming pool appear shallower than it really is?
mcqs.why: Rays from the bottom of the pool bend away as they leave the water, making the bottom appear raised and the pool shallower.

mcqs.q: Dispersion of white light means:
options: Splitting of white light into seven colours
mcqs.why: Dispersion is the splitting of white light into violet, indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange and red when it passes through a prism.

mcqs.q: In dispersion through a prism, which colour bends the most?
mcqs.why: Violet light is refracted the most in glass and red the least, which is why the colours separate into a spectrum.

mcqs.q: How can white light be obtained again after a prism disperses it?
options: By passing it through a glass slab only
By placing a second prism upside down close to the first
By reflecting it in a plane mirror
mcqs.why: The inverted second prism bends the separated colours in the opposite way and recombines them into white light, as Newton showed.

mcqs.q: Why is there no net dispersion through a glass slab?
options: Its surfaces are inclined to each other
Its surfaces are parallel and colours recombine at the second surface
Glass does not refract light at all
mcqs.why: In a slab the colours bend at the first surface but bend back equally at the parallel second surface, so they emerge together as white light.

mcqs.q: Which two conditions are necessary for the formation of a rainbow?
options: Clouds and a high Sun at noon
Water droplets in air and Sun behind the observer
A prism and a dark room
mcqs.why: Raindrops disperse sunlight like tiny prisms, and the Sun must be low behind the observer for the colours to reach the eyes.

mcqs.q: Why is a rainbow not seen at noon?
options: There is no moisture at noon
The Sun is too high for the dispersed light to reach our eyes
Raindrops do not act as prisms at noon
White light has no colours at noon
mcqs.why: A rainbow needs the Sun low, below about 42 degrees; at noon the geometry fails and dispersed light is directed below the horizon.

mcqs.q: Stars appear to twinkle mainly due to:
mcqs.why: Starlight bends again and again while passing through moving layers of air, so the star appears to twinkle.

lessons.title: Electric Circuits: Open and Closed
lessons.notes_html:
Electric Current and Circuit

Electric current is the flow of electric charge, that is electrons, through a conductor. Its SI unit is the ampere. An electric circuit is the complete path along which electric charge flows. It is made of a source such as a cell or battery, connecting wires and devices.

Closed and Open Circuits

In a closed circuit the path of current is complete. The cell, wires, bulb and switch are all connected with no break, so current flows and the bulb glows. A closed circuit is the complete path of electric current.

In an open circuit the path is broken at some point, for example the switch is open. No current flows and the bulb does not glow.

The Electric Switch and Dimmer

An electric switch is a device used to make or break a circuit. When the switch is off, it creates a gap and the circuit is open. When the switch is on, it joins the two ends, completes the path, and the circuit is closed.

A dimmer switch contains a variable resistance. With more resistance, less current flows and the bulb glows dim. With less resistance, more current flows and the same bulb glows bright. So the dimmer controls brightness by controlling the current.

Circuits at Home and the Bicycle Dynamo

A parallel circuit is used in home supply. Every appliance gets the full supply voltage, each appliance can be switched on or off independently, and if one appliance is faulty the others keep working.

In a bicycle dynamo system, the rotating wheel has mechanical energy from pedalling. The dynamo converts it into electrical energy when the wheel spins a magnet inside a coil. The lamp then converts electrical energy into light energy with a little heat.

Key Points

  • Electric current is the flow of charge and its unit is the ampere.
  • A closed circuit has a complete path, so current flows and the bulb glows.
  • A switch makes or breaks a circuit, and a dimmer controls current.
  • Homes use parallel circuits so appliances work independently.

mcqs.q: An electric circuit is the path along which:
options: Electrons revolve around the nucleus of an atom
mcqs.why: An electric circuit provides the complete path through which electric charge flows from the source through wires and devices.

mcqs.q: A closed circuit is the:
options: Path with a gap at the switch
mcqs.why: In a closed circuit there is no break in the loop, so the path is complete and current can flow through it.

mcqs.q: What is electric current?
options: The flow of electric charge through a conductor
A coil that acts as a magnet
The path made by wires only
mcqs.why: Electric current is defined as the flow of electric charge, that is electrons, through a conductor, measured in amperes.

mcqs.q: What is the SI unit of electric current?
mcqs.why: The ampere, written as A, is the SI unit used to measure the amount of electric current flowing in a circuit.

mcqs.q: In an open circuit, why does the bulb not glow?
options: The path is broken so no current flows
The cell produces too much current
The wires absorb all the charge
mcqs.why: An open circuit has a gap, usually at the open switch, so charge cannot complete the loop and the bulb stays off.

mcqs.q: What does an electric switch do in a circuit?
options: It increases the voltage of the cell
It makes or breaks the circuit
mcqs.why: A switch joins the ends to close the circuit and let current flow, or creates a gap to open the circuit and stop the current.

mcqs.q: How does a dimmer switch make a bulb glow dim?
options: By increasing the current in the bulb
By adding more resistance so less current flows
By changing the colour of the bulb
mcqs.why: The dimmer has a variable resistance; more resistance reduces the current through the bulb, so the same bulb glows dim.

mcqs.q: Which type of circuit is used in home supply?
mcqs.why: In parallel wiring every appliance gets full voltage and can work independently, and one faulty appliance does not stop the others.

mcqs.q: In a bicycle dynamo, the dynamo converts mechanical energy into:
mcqs.why: The turning wheel spins a magnet inside the coil of the dynamo, converting mechanical energy into electrical energy for the lamp.

mcqs.q: In a closed circuit with a cell, switch and bulb all connected, the bulb glows because:
options: The path is complete and current flows
The switch creates a gap in the path
The wires store the light energy
The cell works without a loop
mcqs.why: With no break in the loop, charge flows from the cell through the bulb, so electrical energy changes into light in the bulb.

lessons.title: Magnetic and Non-magnetic Materials
lessons.notes_html:
Magnetic Materials

Magnetic materials are attracted by a magnet. Important examples are iron, steel, nickel and cobalt. These materials can be used to make magnets and electromagnet cores.

Non-magnetic Materials

Non-magnetic materials are not attracted by a magnet. Examples include silver, gold, glass, marble, wood, plastic, rubber, copper and aluminium. Silver is a non-magnetic substance, while cobalt is a magnetic substance.

Magnetic Field

The magnetic field is the region around a magnet, or around a current-carrying conductor, in which its magnetic force can be detected. A magnet can attract magnetic materials placed within its field.

Testing Whether a Bar Is a Magnet

Attraction alone does not prove that a metal bar is a magnet, because a magnet also attracts unmagnetised iron or steel. The sure test is repulsion. Bring one pole of a known magnet near both ends of the bar. If one end is attracted and the other end is repelled by the same pole, the bar is a magnet. If both ends are only attracted, the bar is just a magnetic material and not a magnet.

Key Points

  • Iron, steel, nickel and cobalt are magnetic materials.
  • Silver, gold, glass, wood and plastic are non-magnetic materials.
  • A magnetic field is the region where magnetic force can be detected.
  • Repulsion is the sure test that a bar is a magnet.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a non-magnetic substance?
mcqs.why: Silver is not attracted by a magnet, while iron, steel and nickel are all magnetic materials attracted by a magnet.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a magnetic substance?
mcqs.why: Cobalt is a magnetic metal attracted by a magnet, whereas glass, marble and gold are non-magnetic materials.

mcqs.q: Which group contains only magnetic materials?
mcqs.why: Iron, steel and nickel are all attracted by a magnet; the other groups list materials that a magnet does not attract.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a non-magnetic material?
mcqs.why: Wood is not attracted by a magnet, so it is non-magnetic, while nickel, cobalt and steel are magnetic materials.

mcqs.q: The region around a magnet in which its magnetic force can be detected is called its:
mcqs.why: The magnetic field is the space around a magnet or current-carrying conductor where its magnetic force can be felt or detected.

mcqs.q: What is the sure test to prove that a metal bar is a magnet?
options: It attracts iron filings at one end
It is repelled by a pole of a known magnet
It is attracted at both ends
mcqs.why: Repulsion occurs only between like poles of two magnets, so repulsion proves the bar itself is a magnet.

mcqs.q: A known magnet pole attracts both ends of an unknown bar. The bar is most likely:
options: Only a magnetic material, not a magnet
mcqs.why: A magnet attracts unmagnetised magnetic material at both ends; a real magnet would show repulsion at one end.

mcqs.q: If bar 2 is a magnet, what will a student observe with one pole of bar 1?
options: Both ends of bar 2 are repelled
Both ends of bar 2 are attracted
One end is attracted and the other end is repelled
mcqs.why: One end of bar 2 has the opposite pole and is attracted, while the other end has a like pole and is repelled by the same pole.

mcqs.q: Which material would NOT be picked up by a magnet?
mcqs.why: Copper is a non-magnetic material and is not attracted by a magnet, unlike iron, steel and nickel objects.

mcqs.q: Plastic, rubber and aluminium are grouped together because they are:
mcqs.why: Plastic, rubber and aluminium are not attracted by a magnet, so they are all non-magnetic materials.

lessons.title: Electromagnets and Their Uses
lessons.notes_html:
What Is an Electromagnet

An electromagnet is a coil of wire wound around a soft iron core which behaves like a magnet only when electric current flows through the coil. The best material for the core is soft iron. When the current stops, the electromagnet loses its magnetism.

Making an Electromagnet Stronger

The strength of an electromagnet increases with the number of turns of the coil. A coil with 50 turns will pick up more paper clips than a coil with 20 turns. The core also matters: wire wound around an iron nail picks up more clips than wire wound around a wooden stick, because the soft iron core greatly increases the strength while wood is non-magnetic and adds nothing.

Electromagnetic Devices

Many daily-life devices work on the magnetic effect of electric current. Three common examples are the electric bell, the electric motor and the loudspeaker. Electromagnetic cranes, generators, relays and MRI machines also use electromagnets.

Electric Bell, Loudspeaker and Motor

In an electric bell, pressing the button sends current through the coil. The coil becomes an electromagnet, attracts the iron armature, and the hammer strikes the gong. The movement breaks the circuit, the magnetism is lost, a spring pulls the armature back, and the process repeats so the bell rings continuously.

In a loudspeaker, varying audio current passes through a coil placed in the field of a permanent magnet. The coil vibrates and makes the attached paper cone vibrate, which produces sound.

In a DC electric motor, current passes through a coil placed in a magnetic field. The coil experiences a force and rotates, converting electrical energy into mechanical energy. Motors are used in fans, toys and many machines.

Key Points

  • An electromagnet works only while current flows through its coil.
  • Soft iron is the best core material for an electromagnet.
  • More turns and an iron core make an electromagnet stronger.
  • Electric bells, motors and loudspeakers use electromagnets.

mcqs.q: The best material to be used as a core in the coils for making an electromagnet is:
mcqs.why: Soft iron becomes strongly magnetised when current flows and loses magnetism quickly when it stops, making it the best core.

mcqs.q: An electromagnet is best defined as:
options: A permanent bar magnet painted red
A coil around a soft iron core that acts as a magnet when current flows
Any piece of iron kept near a magnet
A coil that works without any current
mcqs.why: An electromagnet needs current in the coil; the soft iron core concentrates the effect and it behaves like a magnet only while current flows.

mcqs.q: Which coil will pick up more paper clips when current passes through it?
options: A coil of wire with 20 turns
A coil of wire with 50 turns
A straight wire with no turns
A coil with the current switched off
mcqs.why: The strength of an electromagnet increases with the number of turns, so 50 turns produce a stronger magnet than 20 turns.

mcqs.q: Which arrangement will pick up more paper clips?
options: Wire wound around a wooden stick
Wire wound around an iron nail
Wire lying straight on the table
Wire wound around a plastic ruler
mcqs.why: The iron nail acts as a soft iron core and greatly increases the strength, while wood and plastic are non-magnetic.

mcqs.q: An electric bell works on which principle?
mcqs.why: Current makes the coil an electromagnet that attracts the armature and hammer, and repeated making and breaking rings the bell.

mcqs.q: In an electric bell, after the hammer strikes the gong, the circuit breaks and the armature is pulled back by:
mcqs.why: When the circuit breaks the electromagnet loses magnetism, so the spring pulls the armature back and completes the circuit again.

mcqs.q: How does a loudspeaker produce sound?
options: A vibrating coil makes the paper cone vibrate
A hammer strikes a metal gong
Air is heated by the current
A magnet spins a fan blade
mcqs.why: Varying audio current in a coil within a permanent magnet field makes the coil and its paper cone vibrate, producing sound.

mcqs.q: Which set lists three electromagnetic devices in daily life?
options: Electric bell, electric motor and loudspeaker
mcqs.why: The bell, motor and loudspeaker all work using electromagnets and the magnetic effect of electric current.

mcqs.q: A DC electric motor converts electrical energy mainly into:
mcqs.why: Current in a coil placed in a magnetic field produces a force that rotates the coil, giving mechanical energy used in fans and toys.

mcqs.q: What happens to an electromagnet when the current through its coil is switched off?
mcqs.why: An electromagnet depends on current in the coil; without current the soft iron core loses its magnetism almost at once.

lessons.title: Soaps and Detergents
lessons.notes_html:
What Is Soap

Soap is the sodium or potassium salt of long chain fatty acids. It is made from natural fats and oils with alkalis. Baking soda, calcium carbonate, glycerin and fluorides are usually used for making toothpaste, not soap.

What Is a Detergent

A detergent is a synthetic cleaning agent made from petroleum products. Soaps are biodegradable, while many detergents decompose slowly.

Difference Between Soap and Detergent

  • Soap does not work well in hard water because it forms scum.
  • Detergent works well in both soft and hard water and does not form scum.
  • Detergents have stronger cleaning action for very dirty and greasy clothes.
  • Detergents can be made for special purposes such as washing machines, dishes and floors.
  • Detergents remain effective even in acidic water, where soaps fail.

Because of these reasons, detergents are considered more useful than soaps in everyday life.

Dry Cleaning

Dry cleaning does not use water or ordinary detergents. Woollen clothes are dry-cleaned with a petroleum solvent such as benzine or petrol. Wool shrinks and loses shape in water, so this solvent dissolves grease and dirt without damaging the woollen fabric.

Key Points

  • Soap is a sodium or potassium salt of long chain fatty acids.
  • Soap forms scum in hard water, but detergent works in hard water.
  • Detergents clean greasy clothes strongly and suit special purposes.
  • Woollen clothes are dry-cleaned with a petroleum solvent, not water.

mcqs.q: Baking soda, calcium carbonate, glycerin, fluorides, etc. are usually used for making:
mcqs.why: These ingredients are the usual components of toothpaste for cleaning teeth, not the fatty acid salts used to make soap.

mcqs.q: Soap is the salt of long chain fatty acids of which metals?
mcqs.why: Soap is defined in the book as the sodium or potassium salt of long chain fatty acids made from fats and alkalis.

mcqs.q: Why does soap not work well in hard water?
options: It forms scum in hard water
mcqs.why: In hard water soap reacts and forms scum, so much soap is wasted and cleaning becomes poor.

mcqs.q: How is a detergent different from a soap in hard water?
options: It works well and does not form scum
It works only in acidic water
mcqs.why: Detergents are synthetic cleaners that remain effective in both soft and hard water without forming scum.

mcqs.q: Detergents are considered more useful than soaps because they:
options: Are made only from natural oils
Work in hard and soft water with strong cleaning action
Can only be used for dishes
mcqs.why: Detergents clean very dirty and greasy clothes, work in hard water and acidic water, and can be made for special purposes.

mcqs.q: Soap is made from which type of starting materials?
options: Natural fats and oils with alkalis
mcqs.why: Soap is produced from natural fats or oils reacting with an alkali to give sodium or potassium salts of fatty acids.

mcqs.q: Detergents are mainly made from:
mcqs.why: Detergents are synthetic cleaning agents manufactured from petroleum products, unlike soaps made from natural fats.

mcqs.q: Which statement about decomposition is correct?
options: Soaps are biodegradable while many detergents decompose slowly
Both decompose at exactly the same rate
mcqs.why: Soaps come from natural materials and break down readily, whereas many synthetic detergents decompose only slowly.

mcqs.q: Woollen clothes are dry-cleaned with:
options: A petroleum solvent such as benzine
mcqs.why: Wool shrinks in water, so dry cleaning uses a petroleum solvent that dissolves grease and dirt without harming the fabric.

mcqs.q: Detergents remain effective even in which condition where soaps fail?
mcqs.why: The book notes that detergents stay effective even in acidic water, while soaps fail to clean properly in such water.

lessons.title: Bio-plastics
lessons.notes_html:
What Is Bio-plastic

Bio-plastic is made from natural biomass, mainly starch from corn, banana peels and sugarcane. It can be moulded into sheets and bags like ordinary plastic, but its raw materials are renewable.

Role of Glycerol

Glycerol acts as a plasticizer in making bio-plastic from starch. It is mixed with the starch to make the material soft, flexible and less brittle, so the bio-plastic can be shaped properly.

Bio-plastic and the Environment

Bio-plastic is environment friendly. It is biodegradable and decomposes in the soil within a short time. Ordinary plastic is made from petroleum, does not decompose for hundreds of years, and pollutes land and water.

Ordinary plastic has very long and strong polymer chains which micro-organisms in soil cannot break down. Bio-plastic is made from natural starch which micro-organisms can digest and break down into water, carbon dioxide and biomass. Bio-plastic does not release harmful chemicals, reduces dependence on petroleum, and keeps land and water clean.

Other Natural Materials

Apart from starch and banana, sugarcane can be used to prepare bio-plastic. Other natural materials include potato starch, corn husks, cassava and vegetable oils.

Key Points

  • Bio-plastic is made mainly from starch of natural biomass.
  • Glycerol is the plasticizer that makes bio-plastic soft and flexible.
  • Bio-plastic is biodegradable, but ordinary plastic lasts for centuries.
  • Sugarcane, potato starch and cassava can also make bio-plastic.

mcqs.q: Bio-plastic is made of:
mcqs.why: Bio-plastic is prepared from the starch of natural biomass such as corn, banana peels and sugarcane.

mcqs.q: What is the role of glycerol in making bio-plastic from starch?
options: It makes the material hard and brittle
It acts as a plasticizer to make it soft and flexible
mcqs.why: Glycerol is mixed with starch as a plasticizer so the bio-plastic becomes soft, flexible and less brittle for moulding.

mcqs.q: Which of plastic and bio-plastic is environment friendly?
mcqs.why: Bio-plastic is made from renewable biomass and is biodegradable, while petroleum plastic pollutes land and water for centuries.

mcqs.q: Why is an ordinary plastic bag not biodegradable?
options: It is made of natural starch
Its long strong polymer chains cannot be broken down by micro-organisms
It is eaten quickly by bacteria
mcqs.why: Petroleum plastic chains resist soil bacteria and fungi, so a bag stays in the environment for hundreds of years.

mcqs.q: Bio-plastic breaks down in soil into:
mcqs.why: Micro-organisms can digest natural starch, breaking bio-plastic down into water, carbon dioxide and biomass.

mcqs.q: Which material, apart from starch and banana, can be used to prepare bio-plastic?
mcqs.why: The book lists sugarcane among biomass sources for bio-plastic, along with corn and banana peels.

mcqs.q: How does bio-plastic help a healthy environment?
options: It is biodegradable and reduces dependence on petroleum
It releases helpful chemicals into rivers
mcqs.why: Bio-plastic decomposes in a short time, releases no harmful chemicals and keeps land and water clean.

mcqs.q: Ordinary plastic is mainly made from:
mcqs.why: Ordinary plastic comes from petroleum chemicals, which is why it is non-renewable and not biodegradable.

mcqs.q: Which list contains only natural materials usable for bio-plastic?
options: Potato starch, corn husks and cassava
mcqs.why: Potato starch, corn husks and cassava are natural plant materials that micro-organisms can break down, suitable for bio-plastic.

mcqs.q: Without glycerol, starch bio-plastic would tend to be:
mcqs.why: Glycerol makes the starch material flexible; without this plasticizer the bio-plastic stays stiff and brittle.

lessons.title: Energy Technology in Daily Life
lessons.notes_html:
UPS and the Inverter

UPS stands for Uninterruptible Power Supply. It is a device containing a battery and an inverter which supplies electricity immediately when the main supply fails, so work on computers and other devices is not interrupted. An inverter is used in a UPS.

A DC to AC inverter converts direct current stored in batteries into alternating current used by household appliances. During load-shedding it lets us run fans, lights, computers and TVs from battery power, and it makes solar energy usable at home.

Advantages of UPS are instant backup power, protection of computers from sudden shutdown and data loss, and protection against voltage surges.
